lecture_summary: The lecture develops waves from familiar oscillators: pendulums and mass–spring systems, restoring forces, and frequency dependence. It then emphasizes particle motion versus wave propagation, transverse and longitudinal waves, spatial versus temporal wave graphs, string-wave speed v = √(F_T/μ), and v = fλ, with brief treatment of reflection, superposition, standing waves, source patterns, membranes, and electromagnetic waves.

videos.title: The Simple Pendulum
videos.reason: Reviews the lecture’s starting oscillator, including simple harmonic motion and calculations involving pendulum period, frequency, length, and gravitational acceleration.

videos.title: Simple Harmonic Motion, Mass Spring System - Amplitude, Frequency, Velocity - Physics Problems
videos.reason: Extends the oscillator model to mass–spring systems and covers restoring force, sinusoidal motion, period, frequency, velocity, and acceleration through representative problems.

videos.title: Mechanical Waves Physics Practice Problems - Basic Introduction
videos.reason: Provides the broadest relevant wave practice: interpreting wave graphs and calculating speed, wavelength, frequency, string tension, and linear density, while also supporting the standing-wave preview.

coverage_gaps: No playlist entry clearly targets the lecture’s central distinction between local particle motion and propagation of the wave pattern, including transverse versus longitudinal waves and compressions versus rarefactions.

The spatial-snapshot versus time-history distinction—y(x) at fixed time versus y(t) at fixed position—and the profile-shifting method for determining a particle’s next motion lack a clearly documented match.
Fixed-end pulse inversion, wave superposition, and their role in producing standing waves are not directly covered by a strong nonredundant match.
Stable versus unstable equilibrium, SHM as projected circular motion, and the vertical-spring equilibrium shift kx_eq = mg are not clearly covered.
The hanging-mass substitution F_T ≈ Mg is not explicitly documented, although the selected mechanical-waves video covers tension and linear density.

Monopole, dipole, and quadrupole sources, membrane modes, and the introductory mechanical-versus-electromagnetic-wave comparison lack appropriately focused matches; the playlist’s electromagnetic-wave video is substantially more advanced than this lecture.
